paragraphs.text: Although the disturbance in the evening troubled us, everyone's eagerness gladdened us. I was not looking at how unruly the commotion was, but at how eager the listeners were. One could see a commotion that was rowdy, like a crowd in the marketplace, but an eagerness that was godly and virtuous, so that one might say, "The hands are the hands of Esau, but the voice is the voice of Jacob." The commotion came from the common crowd, but the zeal came from God. We should not be put out at all by the shouting of the eager, but should look to the zeal of the listeners. The Canaanite woman too cried out after the Savior, yet he did not look at how unruly her shouting was, but at how earnest her mind was. She cried out, then, as you have just heard, following in the Master's footsteps: "Son of David, have mercy on me." Oh, the faith of the Gentiles! Oh, the ingratitude of the Jews! The Canaanite woman, cut off from the race of Israel, who was neither raised under the Law nor lived among the prophets, proclaims the truth, saying, "Son of David, have mercy on me." But those who were raised under the Law and heard the prophets deny the truth and champion a lie, saying, "We do not know him; he is a Samaritan and has a demon." Oh, the faith of the Gentiles! Oh, the ingratitude of the Israelites! See how the God and Master of all honors their race: "It is not good to take the children's bread and throw it to the little dogs." He calls the Gentiles dogs and the Israelites sons, but the people turn the honor upside down. Those who are honored dishonor him, and those who are dishonored worship him. Those called sons do not accept his kindness, while the Canaanite woman, who is named a dog, does not leave her benefactor. This is why the Savior called the woman a dog: not to insult her, but to lay bare her resolve, and to show that the Gentiles do not leave their benefactor even when they are insulted, whereas Israel denied the Savior even when he was doing them good. "Son of David, have mercy on me." And he who hears everyone is silent. He is not rejecting her plea, but making her faith shine more brightly. She was a Canaanite by race and a daughter of Abraham by faith. "Son of David, have mercy on me." And he who hears the pleas of souls before their mouths cry out is silent and holds back. To the apostles he seemed harsh for turning away so earnest a plea. The disciples said to him, "Send her away, for she is crying out after us." So are you, Peter, or you, Andrew, or you, Philip, kinder than the Savior? Did her pleading move you, while her plea did not move him? "You judge by appearances," he says, "but I judge by intentions. I put off and delay the favor so that I may lay bare her splendid faith." "I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel." So then, are you the shepherd of the Israelites alone, and not the Master, Shepherd, Ruler and Provider of the whole earth? He did not say, "I am not the shepherd of the others," but, "I was not sent for this." He did not say it because it was true. Rather, he took this stance in order to lay bare her faith. For if you were sent nowhere else but to the sheep of the house of Israel, how do you send the apostles to the ends of the earth, saying, "Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them"? If you were not sent to the other sheep but only to those of Israel, how could you tell the apostles, "I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd"? So for the moment he is not telling her the exact truth of the matter, but testing her soul. "I was not sent." He refuses the request, yet the woman does not run away but keeps pleading. He shakes off her plea, but she does not shake off her worship of him. Truly the Canaanite woman is an image of the Church. The Church is tested in dangers and does not deny the Master. It endures countless storms and keeps its eye on the harbor of faith. It is tossed by countless waves of heretics and is not shaken from its firm faith. Compare the faith of the Church with the ingratitude of the Jews. The Jews grumbled while they ate manna; the Church fasts and gives thanks to the Master. They are ungrateful when they are honored; Christ's people give thanks when they are persecuted. If you were a master, which servant would you approve? Of two servants, which would you approve: the one who is ungrateful after receiving kindness, or the one who is grateful under discipline? The Canaanite woman, then, is an image of this Church: she is sent away and yet does not deny the Master. She worships him, saying, "Lord, help me." At first she had said, "Son of David, have mercy on me." Thinking that her plea had fallen short of his dignity, she takes back her first words and covers them with a second, more fitting acknowledgment. She no longer calls him "Son of David," but Lord, saying, "Lord, help me." Still he does not answer, and the apostles are annoyed by her voice, saying, "She is crying out after us." God delays, with his eye on her faith, and says to her, "It is not good to take the children's bread and throw it to the little dogs." In calling the Israelites children, he is not so much honoring them as rebuking them for their ingratitude. For the one who today calls the Israelites children is the Son of the one who says, "I have begotten sons and raised them up, but they have rejected me." The Canaanite woman is called a dog and bears the insult graciously. Yet I think, and believe, that within this insult he placed an image of loyalty. He said "dog" to point to the loyalty of that animal. Even when a dog suffers countless hardships, it does not leave its master's house. When a dog sees its master's footsteps, it is silent. When it sees its master's servants, it stays quiet. But when it sees strangers, it grows wild, barks and will not be quiet, paying no attention to anything else. How can the Jews see countless blasphemies against God and not be disturbed? Look at a Christian who hears a heretic's blasphemy or some other error. He is at once stirred up, barking and shouting against the opponents. A Christian cannot bear to see a stranger's face, but barks like a dog at his master's gate. Even the philosophers outside the faith gladly took the name of dogs because of the animal's loyalty. They were not ashamed of the name, but looked to the loyalty of its nature. God approves of those who bark on behalf of true religion and blames those who are silent and do not bark for the truth. That is why he says of the Israelites, "They are all mute dogs, unable to bark." A soul that is loyal to the Master and barks on the Master's behalf is called a dog, and this is no insult. When a dog goes mad, its only sign of madness is that it bares its teeth against its master. A dog in its right mind never rages against its master. Nothing proves the madness of the Jews more than their barking against the Savior. They should have recognized God as their Master, but they shook him off as a stranger. That is why he accuses them, saying, "Many dogs have surrounded me." And who are the dogs? "A gathering of evildoers has encircled me." So the Canaanite woman does not reject the insult, but accepts it with thanks. "It is not good to take the children's bread and throw it to the little dogs." And she makes the insult into a plea for kindness, saying, "Yes, Lord, for even the little dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters' table. Do not pity me as a child, but have mercy on me as a dog. I accept your insult, Master. An insult from you is better than any honor and higher than any glory." The Savior wanted to show in the end that he had not called her a dog to insult her. So when he had laid bare her thankfulness, he said, "O woman, great is your faith. Let it be done for you as you wish." I do not know how to praise the faith that the Savior called great. What better praise could I devise than the praise the Savior gave? Let us leave his words untouched. Let us not insult them with our own praises, and let us not make what is great small. Human praise diminishes things, but the voice of God bears witness to them. "Their praise," it says, "is not from men but from God." But why did those troubled by demons call on the Savior for help at all, saying, "Son of David, have mercy on me"? Does kinship with David have power over demons? Why did the one who was prophesying cry out at all, "Son of David, have mercy on me"? And why did the Canaanite woman, bringing her daughter who was possessed by a demon, say, "Son of David, have mercy on me"? The historical account tells us that David drove the demon away from Saul by playing the holy lyre in measured strains. David, then, drove out demons by the power of music, and not human music but divine music, played by the Holy Spirit. So they took a title of praise from this kinship and said, "Son of David, have mercy on me." However, we should not stop at this title. We should let it guide us, but rise above it to his true dignity. "Her child was healed from that hour." The voice of God went out and healed the child. The Savior's voice banishes demons and drives out every hostile condition.

But enough on the grace of the Gospel. We have not said as much as should have been said, only as much as we were able to say. Since we cannot pay all that we owe, let us turn to our promise, so that we do not dull the longing of those eager to hear by putting it off day after day. It is time, then, for me to take up my promise and pay you the hearing I owe you. Our discussion was about Pharaoh: how God hardened Pharaoh's heart. It was also about the saying, "He has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills. You will say to me, then, 'Why does he still find fault? For who has resisted his will?'" Those who handle divine thoughts, and those who listen to them, must not rush straight to the interpretation, or the meaning will seem forced. They must take up the subject of the grace of the Gospel from the beginning, so that by following the sequence I may give you a clear and orderly explanation. To be brief, then, I will begin my discourse here. The passage is in the Epistle to the Romans. Paul writes to the Romans with many other exhortations as well, but above all to correct a matter that was causing much trouble and disorder. Hear how it came about. In Rome many Jews had come to believe in the Savior, and many Gentiles had believed too. There was strife and uproar between the two parties, not from zeal for true religion but from rivalry over first place. Those from the Gentiles wanted to be thought first, and those from the Jews also wanted to be first. Those from the Jews brought forward their ancestral nobility and said to those from the Gentiles, "We are more honorable than you. Our religion is older, and the patriarchs are ours: Abraham is ours, Isaac is ours, Jacob is ours, and so are all the patriarchs and the prophets. Our nobility is ancient, but you received this kindness only recently." Those from the Greeks said, "Those who denied Christ cannot hold first place. Those who set up the cross and fought against God cannot be ranked in the first class. You were cast off, and all the nations were called. We are the ones who seized the kindness, and you are the ones who insulted it." The apostle saw that great disturbance and uproar had come to a head in Rome. He reflected that an evil growing in the great city could spread everywhere under heaven. So he cut the rivalry back at its root, as it were, so that it would not spread from there into the whole earth. He placed himself in the middle and acted not as a judge but as a peacemaker, knowing that rivalry does not establish true religion, while true religion dissolves all rivalry. Those who want to quell a fight and an uproar do not rebuke one side only, lest they inflame the other side further. They rebuke both, so that their rebukes make their advice welcome and effective. In the same way the divine apostle placed himself between the combatants and quelled both the clamor of the Jews and that of the Gentiles. He attacks the more shameless party first, I mean the Jews. "For they are all shameless dogs, unable to bark." They are a shameless people. I do not say this because of their race, but because of their character. It is not low birth that is shameless; it is conduct that is base. So he censures this party, or rather attacks it first, this shameless party, to whom Isaiah said, "Your neck is iron and your forehead is bronze." That is how shameless he knew it to be. And the prophet Jeremiah says, "You had the face of a prostitute, Israel; you were shameless toward everyone." So the divine apostle attacks the shameless party first, I mean the Jewish party. Since they brought forward the antiquity of their fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, he shows them that one should take pride not in one's race but in one's conduct. That is why he began this discussion by saying, "Not all who are descended from Israel are Israel." Since you put forward your race without showing your conduct, not all who are descended from Israel are Israel. This was said to the Jews. "Nor are they all children because they are Abraham's seed. For it is written: 'Through Isaac your seed shall be named.'" If race produced true religion, nothing would have prevented Israel [?] from being preferred to Isaac. For he was a son of Isaac [?]. For he was a son of Abraham, and the elder son. So "not all who are descended from Israel are Israel, nor are they all children of Abraham because they are Abraham's seed; but through Isaac your seed shall be named." And Paul adds the explanation: that is, it is not the children of the flesh who are counted for faith, but the children of the promise; these are the children of God. But a Jew might push back against this statement and bring another piece of shamelessness against the divine message. He might say that Ishmael was rejected because he was born of a slave woman, while Isaac was preferred because he had the nobility of being born of a free woman. So he [?] then brings in a counter-example, saying, "Not only Isaac, but also Rebecca, when she had conceived by one man, our father Isaac. For before they were born or had done anything good or bad, so that God's purpose in election might stand, not from works but from him who calls, she was told, 'The elder will serve the younger.'" Since there you bring forward a low birth according to the flesh to fuel your rivalry, I show you two branches split from one root. I show you that the one who was not expected was accepted, and the one who was expected was not accepted. Nature does not disgrace one whom his own choice does not disgrace. This is so that you may learn that it was said, "The elder will serve the younger," as it is written: "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated." Paul draws this from the divine voice. For God says through the prophet, "Was not Esau Jacob's brother? Yet Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated." "Since you put forward nature," he says, "what good did nature do Esau? Since the nobility of one's fathers is a source of pride, what more did Esau gain from his father's nobility? Was he not a descendant of Abraham? Was he not the son of Isaac? Was he not born of the same mother? Was he not of the same free birth? Did his race do him any good, when his character cast him out?" At once he adds, "What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? By no means!" Up to this point he has dealt with the history. Now he arms himself against the objection that arises. Many people, while one subject is being examined, seize on incidental remarks as grounds for slander. So the apostle looked not only to the rivalry of those who were fighting at the time, but also to the strife of those who would arise later: Manichaeans, or heretics, or pagans who would arm themselves against this passage. He prepares his arrows in advance, to store up weapons for you for the height of the battle. For God does not see only the present; much more does he foresee the future. That is why the word of God is called an arrow and a sword. Isaiah says, "He made me like a sharp sword and hid me in his hand. He made me like a choice arrow; he covered me in his quiver." Why a sword and an arrow? A sword is used against those standing nearby, but an arrow is shot even at those standing far off. The word of God put down the rivalries of that time, and it also cut short the quibbles that would arise in the future. So it is called a sword that fights those nearby, and an arrow shot at opponents standing far off. But so as not to break the thread of our subject, let us first say those things and then come to these. Once he had restrained the Jews from being proud of their race, he immediately takes up those who came from the Greeks and says to them, "Do not boast over the root. For you, a wild olive, were cut from the olive that is wild by nature and grafted into the cultivated olive." Whoever reads the epistle carefully will find the solution there in full, but we will take the short way. He calls the Israelite race the cultivated olive, and he restrains the Gentiles who were cut from the wild olive and grafted into the cultivated one. He calls the race of Abraham the cultivated olive, and he restrains those who came from the Gentiles and tasted the sweetness of Abraham and the prophets from thinking too highly of themselves. "Was Israel grafted into you?" he says. "Did you receive Israel? Did Israel not receive you? Did the apostles come from you? The Savior came from the Jews, not from the Gentiles. From the Jews! Why then do you forget the root of your blessings and give yourself airs? Do you not know that you, a wild olive, were grafted into the cultivated olive?" But you will surely say to me, taking up the opponent's fight again, "They were broken off for their unbelief, but I was grafted in by faith." "Well said. Do not be proud, but fear. For if God did not spare the natural branches, perhaps he will not spare you either." See the apostle's voice! See the apostle's bowstring! See how he cuts out the rivalry root and all, silencing one side and shaming the other. "Do not be puffed up. If you boast, remember that it is not you who support the root, but the root that supports you." Those from the Gentiles were boasting over Israel, as though Israel had been cut off for fighting against God in Christ, while they themselves had been called back through knowledge. So to those who were being so bold he says, "It is not you who support the root, but the root that supports you." "But you will say, 'They were broken off so that I might be grafted in.'" "I gladly agree with what you say; I accept your grateful answer. Well said. But do not be proud; fear instead. For if God did not spare the natural branches, perhaps he will not spare you either." He cast off the one who had nobility by nature because of his unbelief; he will cast you off for your arrogance, because of the same ingratitude. And see how he drives out rivalry through fear. "Consider, then, the kindness and the severity of God: severity toward those who fell, but kindness toward you, if you continue in his kindness. Otherwise you too will be cut off." See how he cuts off rivalry by fear, and leads the believer not to compete with others but to strive anxiously himself. Why do you busy yourself with someone else's race? Strive for your own life. Be eager to please your benefactor. Do not betray your nobility by your conduct. Then those from the Gentiles say, "Paul was sent to us. He is not yours, you Jews, but a herald to the nations." To this claim Isaiah [?] again applies a saving remedy of true religion: "Do you take pride in me? Yes, I am your teacher and not the Jews'. But learn the exact truth. 'I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that inasmuch as I am the apostle of the Gentiles, I will glorify my ministry.'" What does "I will glorify" mean? I commend my ministry by commending the Gentiles. Why commend them? "In the hope that I may somehow make my own flesh jealous and save some of them." I admire you so that I may stir them to jealousy. With words like these Paul quenches the blazing rivalry and brings in the shining truth. He cuts out what feeds rivalry and brings in what makes for harmony. But let us come to the matter before us.

"What shall we say? Is there injustice with God? By no means! For he says to Moses, 'I will have mercy on whom I will, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.'" Paul does not say these words in his own person, for they follow the line of an objection. Paul, then, gives shape to an objection voiced by those who were quarreling: "What shall we say? Is there injustice with God (by no means!) when he says, 'I will have mercy on whom I will, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion'?" The objection is not given in one unbroken sequence; the "By no means" is a parenthesis. Before he settles the dispute, he at once puts a stop to the blasphemy. While someone is still examining the word, he might pass sentence on God too soon. To prevent this, Paul, like a wise physician, inserts "By no means" in the middle, so that by forbidding the impious thought he may keep the truth from being blasphemed. This is what the objector says: "Concerning Jacob he said, 'Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated'; and to Moses he said, 'I will have mercy on whom I will, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.' If he has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills, why does he still find fault? If he himself does this and he himself brings it about, why does he demand an account from me for what he himself does?" That is the whole force of the objection. "For he says to Moses, 'I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.'" So, as though someone else were objecting and drawing a conclusion from a syllogism, he added, "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated." He added another saying as well: "He has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills." So the objector, as one who has gathered up the argument, says this: "So then it depends not on the one who wills, nor on the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy. If, then, he has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills, if he loves whom he wills and hates whom he wills, what charge do you bring against me? It is in vain, then, that I practice piety; in vain that I run toward the truth. For it depends not on the one who runs, nor on the one who wills, but on God who shows mercy." All this is spoken in the person of the objector. And from here on the apostle does not hesitate to resist him strongly. He does not wish to confirm the objection; he wishes to clear away every suspicion held by the Gentiles. "So then he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills. You will say to me then, 'Why does he still find fault? For who has resisted his will?'" Then Paul begins his reply, saying, "No indeed, O man, who are you to answer back to God?" Here there is no resolution of the objection. There is first indignation against those who dare to dispute with God. To silence the objector is not to resolve the question; it only increases the perplexity. "If you rebuked me for saying what is just, I fall silent and submit to your authority. But why do you accuse me instead of persuading me?" Yet first he silences the boldness of human rashness, which dares, and is altogether eager, to receive from God [?] an account of what happens: "No indeed, O man, who are you to answer back to God?" And he takes a common example, for ideas must also be grounded in ordinary experience. Suppose someone saw a master beating his own servant, came forward between them and said, "Why are you beating him?" And the master, holding out his authority as master, said, "What is that to you? Do I not have authority over my own servant? Is he not mine? Is he not subject to my authority?" These are the words of one asserting his authority, not of one explaining his reasons. To the one who interferes, the angry man at once says, "What is it to you?" But when he has digested his anger and calmed his indignation and become gentle, he then makes his defense to his accuser: "So that you may not condemn me, sir, for beating him without cause, learn what he dared to do." The apostle does the same. The objectors were demanding an account from him: "Since he has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills, why then does he still find fault? For who has resisted his will?" When he saw that the saying was irreverent, he says, "No indeed, O man, who are you to answer back to God?" Does the clay lay down the law for the potter? Does the thing made pry into the one who made it? Does the slave demand an account from the master? Are you not taught even by ordinary affairs? Even a servant who is fighting for his freedom, when he is being dragged into slavery, does not dare to appear in his own person. He takes someone else to plead his case with him, so as not to set a slave's face directly against his master's. And you, a mortal man, measure yourself against the immortal presence? "Who are you to answer back to God?" Do you, a creature of time, pry into the eternal one? The mortal into the immortal? One who will dissolve in the tomb into the one who dwells in heaven? Do you, who are fed from the earth and return to the earth, demand an account from the one who endures through all the ages? "No indeed, O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the potter not have authority to make from the same lump of clay one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?" "Yes," he says, "you silence me well, but you do not resolve the question. By the very means you use to silence me, you add to the charge. For he said, 'Does the potter not have authority to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?' So it is he who makes the dishonored ones as well. Why, then, do you still find fault with me? I cannot accept this saying of yours. By not resolving the charge, you increase the perplexity." Therefore the apostle, having rebuked them as rash, then corrects them as mistaken. In indignation he says, "No indeed, O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the potter not have authority to make from the same lump of clay vessels, some for honor and some for dishonor?" But when he perceived that by silencing them he was rather adding to the objection, he at once goes on: "What if God, wishing to show his wrath and to make known his power, endured with much patience..." Let the words be examined one by one, for the truth cannot be grasped from bare words. He showed and taught that one must not demand an account from God, and Paul made use of the word of God spoken through Isaiah. For God says to the ancient people: "Shall the thing formed say to the one who formed it, 'Why did you make me?' Does the clay answer the potter, 'What are you doing?' Does the thing formed answer the one who formed it, 'Why did you make me?' Yet you give me orders concerning my works and my sons." Paul takes up the silencing words of Isaiah and corrects the mistaken opinions. So the part that rebukes has been shown; let the part that resolves follow. Then you may learn, brother, that Paul brought in "Who are you to answer back to God?" not to settle the questions precisely but out of indignation. Here he ascribes everything to the potter and says, "Does the potter not have authority to make from the same lump of clay vessels, some for honor and some for dishonor?" Here he is speaking against an objection, not stating doctrine with precision. But elsewhere he wishes to show that a vessel of honor and a vessel of dishonor are not made by God. They are made by the free choice of those who act, as it either leans toward what is base or looks toward virtue. There he says to Timothy: "I write these things to you so that you may know how one ought to conduct oneself in the house of God. In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and of clay." These are the words of the same Paul. I do not bring in testimony from elsewhere, so that you cannot say, "Finding no solution in the apostle, he jumped to another scripture." The same Paul who was indignant with these people speaks with precision when he speaks without indignation. So Paul says: "In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and of clay, some for honor and some for dishonor." And what does he add? "If anyone cleanses himself, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified." Here he ascribed the vessel of honor and the vessel of dishonor to the potter; in another place he has attributed the whole thing to free choice: "If anyone cleanses himself, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified and useful to the master, prepared for every good work." See how he speaks one way when he rebukes, and sets things out another way when he teaches. It is like the earlier image of the master beating his own servant, who spoke harshly at once to the outsider and afterward led him on to the truth. So here too he showed that God does not make a vessel of honor and a vessel of dishonor. God makes nature common to all; it is free choice that divides what was created. Scripture teaches us this, so that you may learn precisely that we were not formed by nature as vessels of honor and vessels of dishonor. If someone was formed this way as a vessel of dishonor, why does scripture teach me to be good? For what I was formed to be by nature, I cannot be changed from. Why does it teach one who is evil by nature to be good? Why does it put the good man on his guard, saying, "Let the one who stands take heed lest he fall"? If he is good by nature, why does it guard one who is already secure? Then consider also what goes with "not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs." If nothing depends on me who wills, why do you preach? If nothing depends on the one who runs, why do you toil? If nothing depends on the one who runs, why did God say, "If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land"? If nothing depends on the one who wills, why did the Savior say, "How often I wanted to gather your children together, and you were not willing"? "Not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs." If nothing depends on the one who runs, why did he say to the Galatians, "You were running well; who hindered you?" If it depends neither on the one who wills nor on the one who runs, why does Paul say, "So I run, not aimlessly"? "Forgetting what lies behind and straining toward what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal." Why do you toil, or why do you run? You said, "not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs." But scripture resolves the ambiguity. It did not depend on Isaac, who willed (for he wanted to bless the firstborn), nor on Esau, who ran to the field, but on God, who showed mercy to Jacob. Not on Esau who willed, nor on Isaac who ran, but on God who showed mercy to Jacob. That is how "not of the one who wills" is resolved. But why, at all, "of God who shows mercy"? For the question still remains: "He has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills." Pay close attention, brother. God foreknows all things. But he foreknows them not as one who shapes the future himself; he foreknows as one who sees in advance what is to come and what will be. Some things he predetermines according to his own plan, and other things he foreknows from our actions. To shape something beforehand is one thing; to know it beforehand is another. If I foreknow that a bad man will be bad, my foreknowledge did not make him bad. Here is an example. I often see a young man left by his parents as heir to a great fortune. I see him avoiding education, living among pleasure-seekers, taken up with the shows, and spending his leisure in a mania for horse races. Looking at him, I say at once, "This man will squander his property in a short time; he is throwing away his father's inheritance." I did not shape it because I foresaw it; I inferred it from his habits. What brings about the outcome is not the foreknowledge of the onlooker but the conduct of the one who lives badly. We often say the same in other matters too, brother. We see someone walking along a slippery road without a staff, and at once we say, "This man is going to slip. He does not know what the ground is like; he is bound to take a fall." Does it follow that because you foretell it, you yourself bring it about?

I do not say this because my foreknowledge is like God's. Rather, I use what belongs to you to teach you about what lies beyond you. Pay close attention. They say that you should learn that God makes people righteous and wicked, since he himself said to Jeremiah: "Before I formed you in the womb I know you, and before you came out of the womb I have sanctified you." And he himself says: "Sinners were estranged from the womb; before they came forth they went astray from the belly; they spoke lies." Do you see, they ask, that from the belly this one was shown to be righteous and that one wicked? Do you see that it is a matter of nature too? Well, it may be answered, did the Savior say to the Jews: "You are in error, because you know neither the scriptures nor the power of God." Read correctly and do not speak perversely. "Before I formed you in the womb I know you, and before you came out of the womb I have sanctified you." Not first "I have sanctified you," but first "I know you," and then "I have sanctified you." Here he showed the foreknowledge first, and only after the foreknowledge the determination. "Before I formed you I know you, and before you came out of the womb I have sanctified you": because I knew you, I have sanctified you. That is why the apostle says: "Those whom he foreknew he also predestined." He did not say "predestined" first, but "foreknew," and then "predestined." I beg you, help this laboring word along with your eagerness. I do not ask this so that you may cheer, for that is not what we seek, as God is my witness. We seek the common benefit. Open wide for me the hearing of your mind. "Before you came out of the womb I have sanctified you" is a lesser thing than what the apostle says. For does the apostle not say of himself and his fellows: "Whom he foreknew, and he chose us beforehand before the foundation of the world"? Jeremiah he knew from the womb, but the apostles he foreknew before the whole world existed, and he did not merely foreknow them but also chose them beforehand. Let us see, then, whether foreknowledge created a nature. If the apostles' being chosen before the foundation of the world creates a nature of righteousness rather than a virtue of free choice, why were men who had been foreknown called while they were tax collectors? Why does Paul persecute? Why do prostitutes hurry into the kingdom? If the prostitute was foreknown as worthy of the kingdom, why did she prostitute herself? If God foreknew Paul, why does foreknowledge not produce a nature? Why did the one foreknown before the foundation of the world become "a blasphemer, a persecutor and an insolent man"? Do you see that foreknowledge does not make a nature, but that it is choice that is foreseen? If foreknowledge made the apostle, why is Matthew collecting taxes? Collecting taxes is idolatry, for the Savior says: "Let him be to you as the tax collector or the Gentile." In this way he ranked tax collecting on a level with idolatry. If, then, Matthew was foreknown, why was it not foreknowledge that made him an apostle, but his choice that turned him toward obedience? Rahab was saved and numbered among the faithful, and clearly God foreknew her as well. How then did she prostitute herself, though she was foreknown? Why was the pearl that had been foreseen lying in the mud? You see the same thing everywhere: nature is neutral, while choice is foreknown by God and comes to light in each person's own way of life. God foresaw what would be, but it was the fruit of the life that made it known. Take the solution from Paul's own words: "Those whom he foreknew and predestined, these he also called; and those whom he called, these he also justified." Why was Judas called and not justified? "Those whom he foreknew and predestined, these he also called." So the fact that the prophet was known from the womb settles nothing beforehand, since in the case of those chosen before the ages it was not nature that followed, but choice that bore witness to the foreknowledge. It has therefore been shown that foreknowledge does not make a nature, unless someone is utterly contentious and shameless toward the truth itself. But why does he build an argument on Pharaoh at all? Because it was said to Pharaoh: "For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth." To make your power known, do you punish a man? To make your might known, do you destroy the innocent? If he is guilty, then blame him. If he is innocent, do not accuse him. What, then, does "that I might show my power in you" mean? Pay attention to me. I will use an illustration that is ancient and true. When the art of medicine first wished to understand human nature and the internal organs, it made use of incisions and dissected living people, so as to provide healing for others. But this was unjust, that some should be slaughtered alive to save others. What, then, did the ancients do? They took those handed over to death for robbery, adultery or poisoning and dissected them alive. In this way they did no wrong to those being punished and still found help for humanity. A man already handed over to punishment for his offenses they dissected alive, so that they might learn how the organs work while they were still quivering. God, then, is like an all-wise physician. For he is a physician who says, "I did not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance," and "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick." He takes Pharaoh, who was already liable to countless punishments for his own offenses, for he was answerable for many sins. The first was blasphemy, when he said, "I do not know the Lord." Blasphemy was the beginning of his evils. The second was his ingratitude toward the people, in condemning a free race to slavery and brickmaking. The third, that he drowned innocent infants in the river. The fourth, that he showed no reverence for the Lord when the Lord was proclaimed to him. The fifth, that he saw wonders and still shamelessly resisted piety. God took this man, who was subject to many evils, and like the best of physicians he dissected him with wonders. He did not punish him all at once so as to kill him. Dissectors, too, punish and at the same time hold back, cutting through the limbs so that they may discover from every part the workings of their science. He subjects Pharaoh to frogs. He arms strange legions against him, legions of frogs and of locusts, to show the surpassing greatness of his power. He did not send an angel from heaven, or the ranks of the cherubim. He does not send the seraphim against those who oppose him. To display his power he musters legions of frogs. There were armies of locusts, with no commander to be seen, led by God's command. Frogs came out of the river to campaign against the enemy of God. Locusts came, which have no power of rational judgment, yet they carried out their Master's command. Gnats and dog-flies came too. God devises many different wonders against him in different ways, dissecting and tormenting his soul, and punishing in different ways a mind that had been impious in different ways. Learn that this is why he cut him up piece by piece instead of punishing him all at once: so that he might show his power through him. As the all-virtuous Wisdom says: "For your all-powerful hand, which created the world, and your unsearchable wisdom were not at a loss to hurl upon them bold lions or newly created, unknown beasts full of rage." Yet he did everything in a way that showed his long-suffering. That is why God says: "So that you may tell your children's children how I made sport of the Egyptians." So God punishes Pharaoh, who had done things that deserved countless punishments, and says to him: "For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth." That is: so that through you I may win others, through you bring others to their senses, through you instruct others. To learn how his dissection benefited others, look at what scripture shows. Once the ark of God was seized by the Philistines. The diviners and all the false prophets came and said to the kings of the Philistines: "Let us send the ark of the God of Israel away from us, and his mighty hand. Do you not know how much the Lord did to the Egyptians? Why should we harden our hearts as Pharaoh hardened his?" What good sense the Gentiles had! You who argue, be ashamed before the words of the Philistines. "Let us not," said the Philistines, "harden our hearts as God hardened Pharaoh's heart." They ascribed the insensibility to Pharaoh himself: why "should we harden our hearts as Pharaoh hardened his?" "Was it not after he had made sport of them that they sent the people away? So now let us appease God." And again, in another battle camp, when the Philistines saw the ark, they say: "Woe to us! This is the harsh God who struck Egypt. Woe to us! Deliver us, Lord." See how Pharaoh brought them to their senses before they had experienced anything themselves. This is what the Philistines cry out. Another foreign woman, Rahab, once a prostitute but now chaste, the one already mentioned, says to the spies: "We know all that the Lord God did to the Egyptians. We heard it, and our heart was humbled, and no breath remained in us, for your God is great in heaven above and on earth below." Do you see that God does not lie when he says, "For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth"? Let the end of the apostle's teaching be the end of our discourse. Paul says: "What if God, wishing to show his wrath and to make his power known, brought wrath upon vessels of wrath with much long-suffering?" He does not say simply that he brought wrath, but that he brought it upon one who deserved wrath. For what does he say? "With much long-suffering he brought wrath upon vessels of wrath." For just as you know [?] ... the apostle says regarding what is: "Finally, brothers, be strong, be strengthened, be made complete." If you are complete by nature, why do you tell me, "Be made complete"? To be made complete means to make yourselves worthy through your conduct. Take the nature of things as your witness. Nature produces wool, but women make the finished work. Indeed, they call the weaving itself, the work itself, a "completed piece." Just as nature supplies the wool and skill completes what nature has provided, so God formed our nature and then handed it over to our free choice. Our nature, then, is wool. It is up to you to make from it a vessel of honor or a vessel of dishonor. You are a dyer. You received wool from nature, and you received choice like a dye. Do you want to dye the wool royal purple? You become a king's son. Did you dye it with deeds of darkness? You become a son of darkness and night. It is not nature that does this; it is choice that works out the difference. None of this happens by necessity, however much the contentious may contend. By God's grace, as far as lay in our power, we have given the solution, so from now on let these questions be stored away in your minds. And pay close attention. If someone objects, oppose him so as to overthrow him with the vessels of his own house. Just because there are vessels set before you in your house, you do not use them all indiscriminately. You know which jar holds wine and which holds vinegar. In the same way God knows which soul is fit for mercy and which soul deserves punishment. This is not because it was made that way, but because it has been fashioned that way by its own way of life. That is why, brother, he calls both those who are punished and those who receive mercy vessels: "What if God, wishing to show his wrath and to make his power known, brought with much long-suffering wrath upon vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, so that he might show the riches of his mercy upon vessels of mercy?" He made the one who received wrath a vessel of wrath, and the one who received kindness a vessel of mercy, to show that each person calls down wrath or mercy upon himself. But perhaps someone will seize on this saying, or rather on the words "vessels of wrath prepared for destruction." So, he says, it does not come from one's way of life; he himself prepared them. But one must understand that being prepared comes not from nature but from choice. Accept this as testimony: being prepared means making oneself, by choice, worthy of punishment or of kindness. For he says [?]: "Yes, I have not studied the scriptures in exact detail, but I have studied the question, so that you may be healed." A patient under a physician's care does not pry into the nature of the drugs; he is eager only to be healed. If the objector says to you, "How did you learn? How were you taught?", say: "How I learned, I know. How I am to explain it, I do not know. I did not do the healing; I was healed, so that my soul stands unwavering." If you see him still arguing, say: "Since I did not become a physician and was not entrusted with medicine, go to the physicians and they will tell you how the drugs help." May we, who are being healed, send up glory to the only physician and wise God. To him be glory and power to the ages of ages. Amen.
